summary: We built an interactive wildfire website that tracks forest fires across Canada, the United States and Russia from 2002 to 2026, using NASA MODIS and VIIRS satellite data. Users pick a country and year, explore fires on a 3D globe, and click any fire to see how hot it burned and how much smoke and carbon dioxide it released. A local risk tool shows how close past fires came to any city, the seasonal smoke odds and preparedness tips, and a 2027–2035 outlook projects what could come next. It addresses the challenge by turning huge, technical satellite datasets into something anyone can explore without coding, and by linking fires to the pollution they cause. This matters because fires are getting worse: hotter, drier seasons bring more fires and dirtier air, as Canada’s record 2023 season showed. Our site helps communities, students, health officials and fire managers understand the risk, spot the warning signs and prepare before the next big fire season
details:
Our project is an interactive wildfire observation site covering Canada, the United States and Russia, using satellite data from MODIS and VIIRS for 2002 to 2026. Users pick a country and year with a slider, then explore wildfire detections on an interactive globe and view details about each fire. Charts show particulate matter and carbon dioxide emissions, as well as each fire’s heat. A local risk estimator lets users choose a city or map location to see historical fire proximity, seasonal smoke odds and preparedness tips. The site also presents an outlook for 2027–2035 based on historical fire trends and a dry-weather stress setting.

The site shows communities, students and decision-makers which forests burn most often and how much smoke pollution they produce. It also shows that hot, dry seasons lead to more fires and more pollution. In Canada, fire-season heat lines up with fire emissions at about 0.7 (where 1 means moving perfectly together), and the record 2023 season was also the hottest and driest. By turning large, technical NASA datasets into something anyone can explore without coding, it can help fire managers, health officials and researchers decide where to focus prevention and air-quality warnings. Our goal is to raise awareness that forest fires are becoming more severe as fire weather worsens, harming both forests and the air people breathe. People can look up their own region, see its fire and pollution history, and learn the warning signs: heat, dry soil and low rain. Long term, this approach could support early warnings for dangerous fire seasons and better planning for forest protection and public health.

We built the site with JavaScript (MapLibre GL JS) and Python, and host it on GitHub Pages. Our main dataset is NASA FIRMS active-fire detections from MODIS Collection 6.1 (2003–2026) and VIIRS S-NPP 375 m (2012–2026). We kept only reliable detections (MODIS confidence of 70% or higher; VIIRS nominal and high confidence). Each fire is named by location: USDA Forest Service National Forests for the USA, ecozones and provinces for Canada, and federal subjects for Russia. MODIS detections were cross-checked against VIIRS. For pollution, we used fire emissions from the Copernicus CAMS Global Fire Assimilation System (via the EU’s Global Wildfire Information System), which is built from NASA MODIS fire power, and assigned each fire its share of 11 pollutants based on its fire power and land-cover type.

We considered many factors while building the project. We filtered detections by confidence, removed false signals from industry and gas flares, and cross-checked the two satellites. We widened the forest definition to include sparse boreal forest in Canada and northern Russia. We handled gaps in time: VIIRS starts in 2012 and had an outage period, so MODIS covers the full span. We named every fire by its location, and we tracked 11 pollutants while accounting for forests, grasslands and croplands burning differently.
